extracted.intended_audience: foreign and domestic patent applicants and their counsel seeking guidance on Japanese patent prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and procedural/quality standards for preparing, filing, prosecuting, opposing, and enforcing patents in Japan (JPO practice), with special notes for foreign/PCT applicants and licensing strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority claim eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant in Japan may claim priority based upon a patent application filed in any other country that is a signatory of the Paris Convention or the TRIPS agreement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming priority provide priority right date and country and priority application number. For PCT national entry, the firm will obtain claims and specification from the PCT publication if published in English; inform the firm of the PCT application number (and publication number for confirmation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Required application contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A Japanese application may be filed with a copy of the specification in English or Japanese, drawings where necessary, and the following information: name and address of inventor(s), name and address of assignee(s), priority right date and country, and priority application number (if assigned).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide complete information at filing to enable priority claims and prosecution; additional PCT-specific handling described above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority document filing deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: A certified priority document must be filed within one year and four months from the first filing date of a priority-based application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exception: when priority is based on an EPO application the priority document need not be filed because of an electronic transfer system between the EPO and the JPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of Attorney requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO does not require a power of attorney for a patent attorney to file a patent application; a power of attorney is required if the invention is finally rejected and appealed, or if the patent is granted, opposed and responded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If such courses of action occur, the firm's policy is to supply a power of attorney form to the client accompanied with instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and translation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Although all JPO proceedings are performed in Japanese, it is possible to file an initial patent application in English; in this case a Japanese translation must be filed within two months of the initial filing date along with an additional fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The filing date is that of the English application, but the Japanese translation is examined. The English specification can be used as a basis for making minor word corrections to the Japanese specification, but the English specification itself may not be amended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic filing and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO facilitates electronic filing of patent applications and charges a substantial data-entry fee for paper applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note: PCT applications may not be filed electronically at the JPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification sufficiency (enablement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The detailed explanation of the invention must describe the invention in a manner sufficiently clear and complete for the invention to be carried out by a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical format recommended: industrial field of application; prior art; problems the invention is to solve; means of solving the problems; embodiments of the invention; effects of the invention. Include as much information as possible because the JPO is very strict about introduction of new matter and rarely allows new claims unless the language is specifically recited in the body of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting and number of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no limit on the number of claims, but each claim beyond the first requires additional official fees for substantive examination and maintenance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of additional fees Japanese patents tend to average fewer claims. Nevertheless, include claims drafted to maximize licensing fees and potential damage awards; include specific claims covering the most profitable uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional-like early filing practice
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO does not have a formal provisional system like the US, but it is possible to file patent applications provisionally in Japan; the first application can satisfy formalities (e.g., existence of a claim) and obtain an earlier filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple claim repeating the title of the invention in claim 1 can satisfy formalities; disclosing the most important embodiment with a simple claim can function like a US provisional. The first application can serve as a priority base for applications filed outside Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT national phase translation and amendment consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The national phase in Japan must be an exact translation of the originally filed PCT application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-filing review of PCT applications is important to ensure preparation with Japanese practice in mind. Cost can be reduced by entering national phase with only the original application and not including PCT Article 19/34 amendments; translations of such amendments are required if filed, but omitting them merely loses the amendments rather than jeopardizing the application. Japanese practice allows ample opportunities for amending during national phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nationalization deadline for PCT
rubrics_metrics.description: The due date for nationalizing the PCT application into Japan is 30 months from the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This applies regardless of whether a Preliminary Examination was requested under the PCT.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication / laying open timing and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications are laid open (published in the Patent Office Official Gazette) 18 months after their filing or priority date, whichever is earlier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After publication any third party may submit relevant prior art to the JPO (information providing practice). Applicants may request early publication under certain conditions (including submission of priority documents and Japanese translation); withdrawal of expedited publication request is not permitted and publication typically occurs about three months after request. Provisional protection based on a published application is available and can be used to send notice letters to potential infringers prior to grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for examination timing and fees
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO will not examine a patent application until a request for examination is filed with official fees, which are based on the number of claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants have three years from the filing date in Japan to file a request for examination. Failure to file by the deadline results in the application being deemed withdrawn with no remedy. A third party may request examination of any laid open patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divisional application practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Divisional applications may be filed (including after allowance if the case has not been appealed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divisional filings may follow steps marked 'Div.'; be aware response periods are shorter for applicants in Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accelerated examination requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Examination can be accelerated for any Japanese patent application having a corresponding foreign application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To accelerate examination, the applicant must provide a copy of at least one search or examination report. When accelerated, a first Office Action is usually issued within about four months (versus about one year or more for normal examination).

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary amendment timing and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Voluntary amendments can be entered before the first office action and within the response period for office actions, provided no new matter is introduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When filing a Request for Appeal, amendments can be filed within 30 days after filing the Appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter prohibition and strictness
rubrics_metrics.description: The JPO will not allow applicants to introduce new matter into the application during prosecution; the definition of new matter is very strict in Japanese practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless specific parallel wording exists in the specification as first filed, it is difficult to add such wording to claims. If the wording can be shown as clearly inferred in the original specification it may sometimes be possible. Include repetitious text using varied terms and expressions in the original specification to provide multiple avenues for future claim amendments. Consider this when drafting PCT applications intended for Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information providing practice (IDS-equivalent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Japan lacks a formal IDS system, but any party may provide a JPO examiner with relevant prior art by providing copies of relevant documents (information providing practice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Potential competitors often alert examiners to prior art. Applicants should also submit prior art cited in search and examination reports in all cases to help ensure a strong patent that will withstand opposition or invalidity trials and facilitate licensing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and inventive step strictness / intermediate concept strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement and inventive step requirements are stricter in Japan than in the US; using an intermediate concept that is narrower than US claims but broader than specific examples helps in obtaining broader Japanese patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such descriptions can be added by filing a domestic priority application similar to a US CIP if filed within one year from the US first priority date. Examples (How, When, What) illustrate drafting intermediate concepts: (1) choose A -> How to choose A; (2) renew -> When to renew; (3) status -> What status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for examiner rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office Action may cite grounds for rejection including: new matter introduced by amendment; applicant is resident of non-reciprocal country; non-statutory subject matter; lack of novelty; lack of inventive step; applicant was not first to file; claimed invention disclosed in a prior application later published; invention contravenes public order/morality/health; application not filed by all joint owners; patent granted contrary to treaty provisions; insufficient description (enablement); allowed claims not supported, clear, concise, and in accordance with patent rules; unity of invention not satisfied; translation issues when English filing followed by Japanese translation; applicant not inventor/no right to obtain a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments in response to a final rejection are limited in scope. The Office Action will list a deadline, usually three months for foreign applicants, within which a response can be filed; a single three-month extension may be automatically obtained. If the examiner remains unconvinced, a second final rejection will be issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of amended novelty law and definition of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese Patent Law section 29(1) was amended to state that a patent cannot be granted for an invention publicly known or practiced beyond Japan’s borders; the definition of publication was broadened to include material publicly distributed over electronic communications networks (such as the internet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public demonstration or sale of an invention abroad before priority filing may bar patent protection in Japan; these changes apply similarly to obviousness requirements under section 29(2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviewing the examiner is often an excellent way to help the examiner understand the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews may result in the examiner suggesting allowable claims and can be an effective prosecution tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal timing and process
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may appeal a decision of rejection; a Notice of Appeal must be filed within 90 days from the final rejection, and any amendments to the application must follow within 30 days after that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary examiner will reconsider the application and new amendments; if still not allowable, the appeal is reviewed by an appeal board typically of three examiners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registration, issue fee, and patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: Once allowance is made and the issue fee is paid, the patent comes into existence as the patent is entered in the Patent Register; a patent number is assigned and a Certificate of Patent is sent to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term of a patent is 20 years from the Japanese filing date. The contents entered in the Patent Register will be published in the Patent Gazette.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opposition after grant
rubrics_metrics.description: After grant, a patent is published for opposition in the Patent Gazette; any third party may file an opposition within six months of publication for opposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds for opposition are similar to examiner rejection grounds, though in opposition certain grounds (joint ownership, unity of invention, claims conforming with patent rules, lack of right to obtain a patent) are not applicable. Opposition hearings are typically before three examiners and the patent owner may be given an opportunity to amend within limits. Consider the opposition period before sending warning letters or timing licensing negotiations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity trial process and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Any third party having a commercial interest adversely affected by a patent may initiate an invalidity trial before the JPO appeal board; these trials are common in Japan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grounds are similar to examiner rejection but some grounds (claims conforming with patent rules and unity) are not available. Additional bases include loss of foreign priority or treaty benefits and failures in corrections meeting statutory requirements. The patent owner may narrow claims through amendment to avoid invalidation; invalidity appeals can delay related infringement litigation and may last two years or more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensing-focused specification drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent specifications should be prepared with an eye toward future favorable licensing terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications filed with licensing goals in mind could be more than twice the number of pages compared to those drafted without licensing considerations because additional language strengthens patents and makes licensing more attractive than litigation. In Japan, all exclusive licenses must be registered with the JPO; after registration the licensee has the right to sue for infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement remedies and indirect infringement standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies for infringement include injunctions and compensation for damages. Indirect infringement occurs when a third party makes, uses, sells, offers to sell, or imports an article that can be used only for the manufacture of a patented product or for working a patented process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it is difficult to prove exclusive use of the technology, indirect infringement is very rarely recognized by Japanese courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of Equivalents criteria (Tsubakimoto precedent)
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused product may be regarded as equivalent to a claimed invention even if a specific claim element is missing when: (1) the element is not an essential feature of the claimed invention; (2) the claimed invention achieved the object and effect even after the element is replaced with a feature in the accused product; (3) the replacement would have been obvious when the accused product was made to a person having ordinary skill in the art; (4) the accused product was not identical to or obvious from the prior art; and (5) the accused product does not correspond to one intentionally excluded from the claim during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This five-factor test stems from the Supreme Court decision in Tsubakimoto Seiki v Tei Eichi Kei (1998) and guides DOE analysis in Japan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic prosecution and enforcement approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Japanese practice and recent law changes trend toward strengthening patent protection; a strategic approach protecting core inventions with an eye toward enforcement and licensing is increasingly important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shared vision with clients and tailoring IP strategies to enforcement/licensing goals (including drafting for licensing and providing strong specification support) will enhance the value of inventions in Japan.
